result:
You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.

Okay. Here.

It's 6:42 a.m. and the kitchen light is the only thing on in the house. The kettle clicks. I am making tea I will not drink. The mug is the chipped blue one from college, the one with the faint ring where my roommate used to put his lip balm. I keep it because throwing it away would feel like admitting that era is over, and I’m not ready for that paperwork.

I keep thinking about how many words a day is normal. How many words is a thought. One hundred. One hundred words is a small paragraph about the weather. One thousand words is a room you can walk around in. It’s enough to describe a childhood bedroom from every angle, to list the things on the nightstand, to remember the way the light hit the dust.

I used to write to fill space. Now I write to find the edges. The first sentence is always the worst because it has to pretend it knows where it’s going. This one is pretending. It doesn’t know. It’s just trying to get permission.

The cat is on the windowsill. She watches the street like it owes her money. A delivery truck sighs past. The fridge hums in B flat. There is a small pile of laundry on the chair I promised I’d fold last week. The socks are mismatched on purpose now. I tell myself it’s aesthetic.

I am thinking about my father’s hands. He was a carpenter. The skin on his knuckles was always split in winter. He would put Vaseline on them at night while watching the news, and the TV light would make his face look younger. He never said “I love you” out loud. He said “Put the milk back in the fridge.” It was the same thing.

There is a particular kind of loneliness that comes with being alone in a house that is full of your own objects. The books you bought and never read. The plant you kept alive for three years and then forgot to water. The mug with the chip. All these witnesses.

I am supposed to write whatever comes to me, so here it is: I am scared of becoming someone who only talks in summaries. Who reduces a year to a bullet point. Who says “it was a good trip” and moves on. I want the granular. I want the way the air smelled at 4 a.m. in that airport. I want the exact color of the plastic cup.

Do you remember the first time you realized you were going to die? I was eight and my dog got hit by a car two streets over. The sound was not like in movies. It was a thud and then a whine. My mother said “He’s gone.” I didn’t understand the verb. I thought she meant he went to the backyard. It took me a whole afternoon to learn what gone meant.

I think about that when people say time heals. Time doesn’t heal. Time just gives you more time to build around the wound. You learn to walk without limping. The limp is still there if you think about it.

I have a list in my phone of things I want to say to people before I die. It’s mostly apologies. A few thank yous. One item says “tell Maya about the lake.” I don’t know why. I haven’t seen Maya in eleven years. Maybe the lake is a code for something I can’t name.

Writing is a way of keeping people alive. Not really, but close enough for the heart. If I write down how your laugh sounded on the phone in 2019, you keep sounding like that for a little while longer. That is selfish and kind at the same time.

The tea is cold now. I should drink it. The steam is gone. Everything is going to be a little less hot than we wanted it to be. That’s not a tragedy. That’s physics.

I keep coming back to the idea of 1000 words as a container. It’s not a lot. It’s not a novel. It’s a postcard from the inside. You can fit a memory, a complaint, a small epiphany, and a question you’re afraid to ask.

So here’s a question: Do you ever miss the version of you that didn’t know things yet? The one who thought love was permanent and work was fair and the body would always cooperate? I miss her competence. She didn’t know better, so she never hesitated.

I have a photo of her on my desk. She’s smiling with braces. She is holding a goldfish bowl. The goldfish is dead in that photo, but she doesn’t know it yet. The bowl is cracked. She thinks the crack is character.

I think about the ethics of remembering. Some memories I polish until they shine. Others I keep scratched on purpose. If I make everything beautiful, I lie. If I make everything ugly, I also lie. The truth is in the grain.

Okay, the cat just knocked a pen off the table. It rolled under the fridge. There goes the metaphor.

I have 200 words left in my head, maybe. I want to say something useful. Here: be gentle with the people who are trying. Most of us are trying so hard we’re exhausted. We want to be good. We want to be kind. We just get tired and snap and then feel bad about snapping.

And also: call your mother. Not because she needs it, necessarily. Because you need the version of you that existed when she sang you to sleep.

The sun is up now. It’s hitting the kitchen counter in a thin white line. The laundry is still on the chair. The mug is still chipped. The cat is still judging the street.

I could keep going. I could write about the first apartment, the fire escape, the neighbor who played saxophone at 2 a.m. I could write about the job I quit, the resignation email I rehearsed in the shower. I could write about the way my hands shake when I’m nervous and how I hide them in my pockets.

But the kettle is off. The tea is cold. The words are doing what they always do: they’re making a small, temporary shelter around the moment. It will hold for a minute. Then the moment will change.

That’s enough. That’s always enough, even when it doesn’t feel like it.

If you were listening, thank you for staying with me this long. If you weren’t, thank you anyway. Words don’t need an audience to be true. They just need a place to land.

I’m going to drink the cold tea now.
